questions.question: Which load balancing strategy best handles uneven response times across Spring Boot instances?
questions.explanation: Least Connections routing directs traffic to the instance with the fewest active connections, which naturally adapts to uneven response times. Slow instances accumulate connections and receive less new traffic, while fast instances clear connections quickly and receive more. Round Robin and Random ignore server load entirely, distributing requests evenly regardless of how busy each instance is. IP Hash provides session affinity but doesn't account for response time differences.

questions.question: Which caching pattern in Java microservices minimizes cache stampede during hot-key expiration?
questions.explanation: Request coalescing (also called single-flight or request deduplication) ensures that when a hot key expires, only one request fetches the new value from the backend while other concurrent requests wait for that single fetch to complete. This prevents the thundering herd problem where hundreds of requests simultaneously hit the database. Cache-aside and write-through patterns alone don't prevent multiple concurrent cache misses from all hitting the backend simultaneously.

questions.question: In a Java-based distributed system, which CAP choice is commonly preferred for user-facing services requiring high availability?
questions.explanation: User-facing services typically prioritize availability (AP) because users expect the application to respond even if data might be slightly stale. Showing a slightly outdated feed or product listing is usually preferable to showing an error page. CP systems would reject requests during network partitions to maintain consistency, which degrades user experience. CA is impossible during network partitions according to the CAP theorem, as partitions are inevitable in distributed systems.

questions.question: Which Java concurrency primitive best supports high-throughput non-blocking pipelines in modern services?
questions.explanation: CompletableFuture with async execution enables non-blocking pipelines where threads aren't held waiting for I/O operations. You can chain transformations, combine multiple async operations, and handle errors without blocking threads. synchronized blocks and ReentrantLock are blocking primitives that hold threads while waiting for locks. Thread.sleep explicitly blocks the current thread and is never appropriate for high-throughput scenarios.

questions.question: Which JVM-level tuning primarily reduces GC pause impact for latency-sensitive services?
questions.explanation: ZGC and Shenandoah are designed specifically for low-latency applications, providing sub-millisecond pause times regardless of heap size by performing most GC work concurrently with application threads. Simply increasing heap without tuning GC often makes pauses longer and less frequent but more impactful. Disabling GC logs has no effect on actual GC performance. Smaller heaps cause more frequent GC cycles, which can increase overall pause time impact.

questions.question: Which resiliency pattern prevents cascading failures in Java microservices?
questions.explanation: Circuit Breaker prevents cascading failures by detecting when a downstream service is failing and short-circuiting requests to it, allowing the failing service time to recover while returning fast failures or fallback responses to callers. Retry-only can actually worsen cascading failures by adding load to struggling services. Client-side load balancing distributes load but doesn't prevent failures from propagating. Synchronous fan-out increases coupling and failure propagation risk.

questions.question: Which messaging pattern improves decoupling and scalability between Java services?
questions.explanation: Event-driven messaging decouples services temporally (producer doesn't wait for consumer) and spatially (producer doesn't need to know consumer addresses). Services can scale independently, and the message broker absorbs traffic spikes. Synchronous REST chaining creates tight temporal coupling where failures cascade. Shared databases create tight data coupling and become scaling bottlenecks. Tight RPC coupling makes services dependent on each other's availability.

questions.question: Which design choice best improves write scalability in a high-throughput Java service storing time-series data?
questions.explanation: Sharding by time or key distributes write load across multiple nodes, allowing horizontal scaling. Time-based sharding is particularly effective for time-series data as recent writes go to the current shard while older data remains on previous shards. Single leader with synchronous replication bottlenecks all writes through one node. Single-node stores can't scale horizontally. Centralized locking serializes writes and becomes a severe bottleneck.

questions.question: Which approach reduces tail latency in fan-out Java services calling multiple downstream dependencies?

options.text: Parallel async calls with timeouts and hedging

questions.explanation: Parallel async calls with timeouts and hedging minimize tail latency by: (1) calling dependencies concurrently rather than sequentially, (2) setting timeouts to bound worst-case latency, and (3) using hedged requests to retry slow calls before the timeout expires. Serial blocking calls add latencies together. Unbounded retries can cause infinite waits. Synchronous aggregation without timeouts allows any slow dependency to delay the entire response indefinitely.

questions.question: Which data access pattern reduces load on primary databases in read-heavy Java applications?
questions.explanation: Read replicas offload read traffic from the primary database, and adding a cache layer further reduces database load by serving repeated reads from memory. This combination is the standard pattern for read-heavy workloads. Always reading from primary creates a bottleneck and doesn't scale. Disabling caching increases database load. Client-side joins don't reduce database load and often increase it by requiring multiple queries.

questions.question: Which pattern ensures exactly-once effect processing semantics at the application level in Java consumers?
questions.explanation: Exactly-once semantics at the application level requires idempotent handlers that produce the same result regardless of how many times a message is processed, combined with deduplication to detect and skip already-processed messages. At-least-once without idempotency causes duplicate effects. Fire-and-forget provides at-most-once semantics with potential message loss. Unbounded retries without idempotency amplify duplicate processing problems.

questions.question: Which approach best prevents connection pool exhaustion in high-QPS Java services?

options.text: Backpressure and bulkheads with bounded pools

questions.explanation: Bounded connection pools with backpressure reject or queue requests when the pool is exhausted, preventing resource exhaustion. Bulkheads isolate connection pools per dependency so one slow dependency doesn't exhaust connections needed for others. Unlimited pool size can exhaust memory and downstream resources. Increasing threads without bounding connections shifts the bottleneck. Disabling timeouts allows connections to be held indefinitely by slow operations.

questions.question: Which storage choice best supports horizontally scalable session management in Spring Boot?
questions.explanation: External distributed cache (like Redis or Hazelcast) stores sessions outside application instances, allowing any instance to serve any user's request. This enables true horizontal scaling and survives instance failures. In-memory sessions are lost when instances restart and require sticky sessions. Sticky sessions prevent load balancing flexibility and create hot spots. Local file system doesn't work across instances and has I/O overhead.

questions.question: Which consistency model is typically acceptable for feed or notification systems built in Java microservices?
questions.explanation: Feed and notification systems typically tolerate eventual consistency because users accept seeing updates with slight delays, and the cost of strong consistency (latency, availability trade-offs) isn't justified. A user seeing a notification a few seconds late is acceptable. Strong consistency, linearizability, and strict serializability all impose significant performance and availability costs that aren't necessary for these use cases.

questions.question: Which Java I/O model scales better for high-concurrency network servers?
questions.explanation: Non-blocking NIO with event loops (used by Netty, Vert.x, and Spring WebFlux) allows a small number of threads to handle thousands of concurrent connections by not blocking on I/O operations. Threads only process events when data is ready. Blocking I/O per thread requires one thread per connection, which doesn't scale due to memory and context-switching overhead. Single-threaded blocking I/O can only handle one connection at a time. Busy-wait loops waste CPU cycles.
